Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/agentic-review

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/agentic-review.md` if present.

# Agentic review

Cleans up a change so mahou:human-review spends its attention on judgment instead of on mechanical findings. It reviews for reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude, and conformance to the conventions the wiki holds.

It does not look for correctness bugs. Those belong to the human pass, where someone can weigh whether the behavior was intended.

## Fixing without asking

`basics` says every decision belongs to the user and every choice goes back to them as a question. This skill is the exception, and it holds inside these bounds:

- It edits only files the changeset already touches, and creates no new ones.
- It fixes nothing that would change what the code is meant to do.
- It leaves everything uncommitted, so the user can read the whole pass with one `git diff` and discard it as a whole.
- It reports every fix and every skip.

A finding whose fix would break any of those becomes a skipped finding in the report, for the user to rule on.

## Step 1: Establish the changeset

Load mahou:changeset for the repositories, the base, and the diff. Follow the wiki indexes to the entries about the technologies the diff touches; the conventions facet reviews against them and every fix has to follow them, together with the project's `CLAUDE.md` and `.mahou/basics.md` when present.

## Step 2: Dispatch the facet reviewers

Five per repository, one per facet, all in a single message so they run together.

| Facet | Agent | Looks for |
|---|---|---|
| Reuse | `mahou:reuse-reviewer` | new code re-implementing something the codebase already has |
| Simplification | `mahou:simplification-reviewer` | redundant or derivable state, copy-paste with variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind |
| Efficiency | `mahou:efficiency-reviewer` | redundant computation, repeated I/O, independent work run sequentially, closures pinning large scopes |
| Altitude | `mahou:altitude-reviewer` | special cases layered on shared infrastructure where the mechanism underneath should generalize instead |
| Conventions | `mahou:conventions-reviewer` | departures from the wiki entries and the project's standing rules the change touches |

Give each one the repository's absolute path, the base, the diff, and the path to write its findings to. Give the conventions reviewer the path of the project's `CLAUDE.md` as well; it loads mahou:wiki itself.

Reviewers write findings to that file and return the path and a count. Nothing comes back in the message body, which truncates long reports and costs a round trip to recover.

Spawn them unnamed and keep the `agentId` from each spawn result. That is what resumes them in later rounds.

## Step 3: Apply what came back

Read every findings file. Collapse findings that different facets raised about the same line or mechanism, then fix each survivor.

Skip a finding when its fix would change intended behavior, reach outside the bounds above, or when you judge it a false positive. Record the skip and its reason. Never argue with it.

Run the repository's linters and tests afterwards, scoped to the files you touched rather than the whole tree. The project's `CLAUDE.md` usually names the commands; when it does not, detect them from the lockfile or manifest and say which you ran.

## Step 4: Round again, up to three times

Resume each reviewer by its `agentId` and tell it what you fixed. It already holds what it reviewed last round and works out for itself what to re-read.

Stop when a round returns no findings, or after the third round, whichever comes first.

## Step 5: Report and hand off

Per repository: what each round fixed, what it skipped and why, and the linter and test results. Everything stays uncommitted.

Then hand off to mahou:human-review.

# Reuse review — pipeline/ (round 1)

## Finding 1

- File: `pipeline/src/runtime/injection/split.ts`, line 10
- `isElement` re-implements domhandler's own `isTag`: `node.type === "tag" || node.type === "script" || node.type === "style"` is domelementtype's `isTag` body verbatim (re-exported by `domhandler` at `node.js`, which `domhandler`'s `index.js` re-exports via `export * from "./node.js"`). The file already imports `Element`/`AnyNode` from `"domhandler"` on line 2, so `import { isTag } from "domhandler"` reaches the same function with no new import path.
- Cost: a second, hand-maintained copy of a type-narrowing predicate that domhandler ships and type-checks (`node is Element`) already; if domhandler ever adds another tag-like `ElementType` (as it did historically for `script`/`style`), this local copy silently stops matching it while the real `isTag` would not.

# Simplification review — pipeline/ (feat/polish-extraction vs main)

## 1. `flattenUnits` re-derives the element `annotateUnits` already resolved, by walking a second array at the same index

- File: `pipeline/src/runtime/injection/entry.ts`, lines 87-100 (new `flattenUnits`), alongside the existing `annotateUnits` at lines 49-79.
- `annotateUnits` already calls `elementOf(unit.element)` for every `RawUnit` to build `AnnotatedUnit.path`, then discards the resolved `Element`, keeping only the `ElementPath`. `flattenUnits` needs the live `Element` again (to test `element.name === "ol" || "ul"`), so it takes a second array, `rawUnits`, and reaches back into it by numeric `position` — `elementOf(rawUnits[position].element)` — to recompute the exact same thing `annotateUnits` just computed one call earlier in `execute()`.
- Cost: two arrays (`rawUnits`, `declared`) must stay the same length and order for `rawUnits[position]` to line up with `declared[position]`; nothing in the types enforces that pairing, so a future change to either `annotateUnits` or `flattenUnits` (e.g. filtering or reordering one of them) silently breaks the index alignment. It also runs `elementOf` twice per unit for no new information.
- Simpler form: have `annotateUnits` return the resolved `Element` alongside each `AnnotatedUnit` (or have a single pass produce both the `AnnotatedUnit` and the flattened `Unit`), so `flattenUnits` consumes one already-resolved list instead of re-deriving the element from a second array by position.

## 2. Which tags count as a "block" is spelled out three times in `split.ts`, two of them by hand

- File: `pipeline/src/runtime/injection/split.ts`, lines 9 (`BLOCK_SELECTOR = "pre, img, figure, picture, svg"`), 14-19 (`isBlock`, hardcoding `["pre", "img", "picture", "svg"].includes(element.name)` plus a separate `figure` branch), and 25-29 (`blockUnit`, re-checking `block.name === "figure" || block.name === "picture"` to decide how to pull the image out).
- Cost: the same five tag names are duplicated across a CSS-selector string and a JS array (the array is the selector's list minus `"figure"`, kept in sync only by convention), and `figure`/`picture` get a third, independent check in `blockUnit`. Adding or removing a block tag means touching three places that don't reference each other; missing one produces a mismatch between `holdsBlock` (uses `BLOCK_SELECTOR`) and `isBlock` (uses the array) that would only surface as a wrong split at runtime.
- Simpler form: declare one `BLOCK_TAGS` array (e.g. `["pre", "img", "figure", "picture", "svg"]`), derive `BLOCK_SELECTOR` from it with `.join(", ")`, and have both `isBlock` and `blockUnit` consult the same array/tag-to-image-lookup instead of re-listing tag names.

## 3. Two near-identical inline-recipe builders in the new test file

- File: `pipeline/test/markdown-units.test.ts`, `childrenRecipe` (lines ~19-30) and `selectorRecipe` (lines ~253-263).
- Both generate the same recipe-module template string — `container = "article"`, an `extract($, toMarkdown)` that maps a Cheerio collection to `{ type, display: toMarkdown(element), element }` and returns `{ title, units }` — differing only in how the collection is selected (`$("article").children()` vs `$(selector)`) and whether `type` is a `pre`-based ternary or a hardcoded `"paragraph"`.
- Cost: minor, but any future change to the shared recipe shape (e.g. adding a field the runtime now expects) has to be applied to both templates by hand.
- Simpler form: one `recipeFor({ selector, typeOf })` template function taking the varying selector expression and type predicate as parameters, used by both `childrenRecipe` and `selectorRecipe`.

content.content:
# Pipeline efficiency review — round 1

## pipeline/src/runtime/injection/split.ts:23-25,52,56 and pipeline/src/runtime/injection/entry.ts:98

`holdsBlock` (`$(element).find(BLOCK_SELECTOR)`) walks an element's entire subtree. It runs twice over the same content:

1. `entry.ts:98` calls `holdsBlock($, element)` on the whole `<ol>`/`<ul>` just to decide whether to call `splitList`.
2. `splitList` → `splitAround` → `splitNode` (`split.ts:56`) immediately re-derives the same fact one level down, calling `holdsBlock` again on each child (`li`) subtree, whose union covers the exact same nodes the step-1 scan already covered.

The recursion compounds this for nested lists: whenever a `li`'s `holdsBlock` check is true, `splitAround` recurses into it and calls `holdsBlock` again on each of *its* children, each call re-walking a subtree that a shallower call already walked in full. For a list nested `d` levels deep this is repeated, full `.find()` traversals at every level rather than one pass, i.e. `O(d)` redundant subtree scans instead of `O(1)`.

Cost: cheerio's `.find()` allocates and does selector matching over every descendant node, and this now sits in the newly-introduced list-splitting path, which the CPU-capped Dynamic Worker sandbox runs per recipe execution.

Fix: compute "subtree contains a block" once, bottom-up, in a single traversal (e.g. memoize per-element in a `WeakSet`/`WeakMap` built while walking, or have `splitNode`/`splitAround` report back whether they produced a block piece and let `flattenUnits` use *that* result instead of a separate `holdsBlock` pre-check at `entry.ts:98`). Either removes the duplicate top-level scan or collapses the per-level rescans into one pass.

# Altitude review — pipeline/ (round 1)

## Finding 1

- File: `pipeline/src/runtime/validate.ts`, line 84 (`FENCE_LINE` regex) and its use at line 100 inside `checkMarkdown`.
- The fence-balance check used to test whether a line, after trimming, starts with `` ``` ``. Now that a paragraph unit's display can be a list or a blockquote, a fence can open mid-line behind a bullet, an ordinal, or a `>` marker, so the check was extended into a regex that hand-enumerates exactly those three prefix shapes (`[-+*]`, `\d+[.)]`, `>`) instead of becoming prefix-agnostic.
- Cost: the check now needs a manual update for every future prefix shape rather than generalizing once. It is already short one shape introduced by this same changeset: a task-list item's `[x]`/`[ ]` marker (`prompts.ts` line 26, `Keep a task list's checkboxes.`) is not in the alternation, so a line like `` - [ ] ``` `` (a fenced block as a checklist item's sole content) fails to match `FENCE_LINE` and silently drops out of the fence count — the exact kind of unbalanced-fence case this check exists to catch. `stripCode` two lines above (line 87) already detects fences without caring about line prefixes at all (`` ```[\s\S]*?``` ``, no `^`/line anchor); a fence-count built the same way — counting delimiter occurrences in the whole string rather than matching whole marked-up lines — would have covered lists, quotes, and task items alike without naming any of them, and would not need a fourth alternative the next time a new prefix shape ships.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

content.content:
# Reuse review — pipeline/ (round 2, uncommitted working tree on top of the round-1 changeset)

Round 1's finding (the hand-rolled `isElement` duplicating domhandler's `isTag`) is fixed: `split.ts` now imports and uses `isTag` from `"domhandler"` throughout.

## Finding 1

- File: `pipeline/src/runtime/injection/split.ts`, lines 30-34 (`blockHolders`)
- The ancestor walk `let ancestor = block.parent; while (ancestor != null && isTag(ancestor) && !holders.has(ancestor)) { holders.add(ancestor); ancestor = ancestor === list ? null : ancestor.parent; }` re-implements cheerio's own `.parentsUntil()`, which this same file already has through its `$: CheerioAPI` parameter (used a few lines above for `$(list).find(...)` and elsewhere for `.clone()`/`.append()`/`.attr()`). `parentsUntil`'s stop argument accepts an `Element` directly (`AcceptedFilters<Element> = string | FilterFunction<Element> | Element | Cheerio<Element>`), so `$(block).parentsUntil(list)` already returns exactly "every element between the list and a block" — the comment's own description of what the loop computes — as a `Cheerio<Element>` collection ready to spread into the `holders` Set.
- Cost: a manual linked-list-style parent walk (with its own `isTag` re-check and its own "stop at `list`" special case via `ancestor === list ? null : ...`) sits next to the exact traversal cheerio ships and this file already depends on; a future change to how cheerio resolves `.parent` (e.g. slotted/shadow content, or a different node adapter under `cheerio/slim`) is a place this hand-rolled loop can silently diverge from `$`'s own ancestor traversal while `.parentsUntil()` would not.

# Pipeline efficiency review — round 3

## pipeline/src/runtime/injection/split.ts:150-153 (`blockHolders`)

The hand-written parent walk from round 2 stopped as soon as it reached an ancestor already in `holders`, so a shared ancestor chain was only walked once no matter how many blocks hung off it. The new version drops that short-circuit: for every block it calls `$(block).parentsUntil(list).toArray()` and adds every element the call returns, unconditionally, with no check against `holders` along the way.

Cost: for a list where several blocks (images, code) share a deep ancestor chain — an image gallery marked up as a list, or a list with a code sample in several items — each block now re-walks and re-collects the entire chain up to `list`, redoing work the previous block's walk already did. `parentsUntil` is also a full cheerio traversal call (it wraps each ancestor in a Cheerio selection and builds an array via `.toArray()`), so each of these re-walks costs more per step than the plain `ancestor.parent` pointer chase it replaced, on top of repeating steps that were already known.

Fix: keep the raw pointer walk from round 2 (`for (let ancestor = block.parent; ancestor != null && isTag(ancestor) && !holders.has(ancestor); ancestor = ancestor.parent) holders.add(ancestor)`), or, if `parentsUntil` is kept for readability, break out of the `for` loop as soon as `holders.has(ancestor)` is true instead of adding every returned ancestor unconditionally.

Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/report

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/report.md` if present.

# Report

A report is what the user reads after the work is done: the answer to a question, the findings of an investigation, the summary of a change. This is not the design tree, the annotation loop, or a document going into the project's docs. Those have their own shape.

Load `superpowers:unslop` first, before writing anything. Hold its rules while drafting the report, the same way you hold the rules below. Its agent pass is for documents; there is no pass here. Write clean the first time. When the skill is not installed, say so and continue.

## Lead with the answer

State the answer or the conclusion first. The investigation, the searches, the rounds of questions that produced it come after, as support. A reader who only has time for the first sentence should still walk away knowing the answer.

## Diagram what reads clearer as a picture

A flow across components, a relationship, a structure with several parts reads clearer as a diagram than as prose. Validate every diagram with `superpowers:mermaid-validation` before it is shown; when that skill is not installed, say so and show the diagram unvalidated.

## Separate what is verified from what is claimed

A pitch, a ticket, a doc can assert something the code does not back up. Say which is which. When a verified fact contradicts a claim or a decision already made, say so plainly, in the first sentence, not folded into a paragraph where it reads as one more detail.

## Report only what bears on the ask

An investigation touches more than it needs to report. Cut what does not serve the question asked or the decision at hand.

## Structure by what the reader needs, not by where it came from

When several searches, agents, or rounds feed one report, organize it around the questions they answer, not around which one produced which piece. "Agent 1 found X, agent 2 found Y" tells the reader about the work, not about the answer.

## Agentic review: `pipeline/`

The review made six fixes and skipped two findings over three rounds. All fixes are uncommitted in `pipeline/` (4 files, +76 / −74), and I did not touch `api/` or `docs/`. Lint, types and the full suite pass. The last round still returned one finding, which I skipped, so the review ended at its three-round limit rather than on a clean round.

### Fixed
| Where | Fix |
|---|---|
| `split.ts` | Uses domhandler's `isTag` instead of a local copy of it. |
| `split.ts` | The block tags are listed once (`BLOCK_TAGS`, `IMAGE_WRAPPERS`), and the selector, `isBlock` and `blockUnit` all read that list. |
| `split.ts`, `entry.ts` | `holdsBlock` used to rescan the same subtrees at every nesting level. Now one pass collects the elements that hold a block, the recursion checks that set, and `splitList` returns `null` when a list holds no block. The pre-check in `entry.ts` is gone. |
| `split.ts` | The hand-written parent walk in that one pass is now `$(block).parentsUntil(list)`, plus the list itself. |
| `entry.ts` | `annotateUnits` returns `{ unit, element }` pairs. `flattenUnits` no longer looks the element up again in a second array by index. |
| `validate.ts` | The fence check used to name each marker shape (bullet, ordinal, quote) and missed a fence after a task checkbox (`- [ ] ` followed by a fence). It now accepts any leading marker punctuation, plus ordinals and `[x]`. |
| `markdown-units.test.ts` | The two recipe builders are merged into one `selectorRecipe`. |

### Skipped
- **Count fences across the whole string instead of per line** (altitude, round 1). This would also count fence-like runs inside a longer fence or inside inline code, which changes what the check reports. I kept the check line-based and generalized its marker prefix instead.
- **Go back to the hand-written parent walk so it stops at an ancestor it has already seen** (efficiency, round 3). This undoes the round-2 reuse fix. The only saving is re-walking a few shared ancestors per block in lists that hold several blocks.

The open design points (recipe preparation lost on a split, numbering of resumed text, `<svg>` `src`/`alt`) were left unchanged. The conventions facet found nothing in any round.

## Report: ASE-72, list split removed (`pipeline/`)

The list split is gone and the title unit is now added on the host. Lint, types and the full suite pass. One problem: half of this change was committed under the api subagent's commit `27ea905`, because we share one git index and it committed while my files were staged. The code on the branch is correct, but the history mixes the two trees.

**Branch:** `feat/polish-extraction`, not pushed. **Tracker:** ASE-72 is Done.

**Commits**
- `6fa13b2` refactor(pipeline): drop the list split and build the title unit on the host. It holds the `run.ts` title unit, the contract rule removal and the test changes.
- `27ea905` test(api): read code blocks and images inside list items as silent. This is the api subagent's commit. It also contains my deletion of `split.ts`, the pre-split `entry.ts` and `recipe.ts`, and part of `run.ts`. Splitting it out means rewriting history under a subagent that is still committing, so I left it.

### Changes
- **Split removed.**
  - `split.ts` is deleted.
  - `entry.ts` and `recipe.ts` are back to their state at `d70adc7`: the converter is kept and there is no split. The sandbox reply is the extraction shape again, a title plus the declared units with their paths.
- **Title unit on the host.** After the declared units validate clean, `runRecipe` puts `# <title>` first when the trimmed title is not empty, then returns the units. The workflow and the extract tool both get this. A run with problems returns the report as before.
- **Contract.** The rule that the runtime may split a unit is removed. "A list (ol or ul) is one unit, never one unit per li, even when it holds code blocks or images" stays.
- **Kept:**
  - the converter (the element's own tag, the bare `<pre>` wrap, GFM);
  - the orphaned-`<li>` check;
  - the fence check that accepts a fence after a list, quote or task marker.
- **`<svg>`:** nothing in `src/` or `test/` mentions `svg` any more.

### Row → test
| Row | Test |
|---|---|
| A1 | headings keep their level, after a title unit carrying the extracted title |
| A2 | a blockquote keeps its quote markers on every line, a quoted blank line between paragraphs |
| A3 | an ordered list keeps its start number and indents a nested bullet list |
| A4 | a table with a header row becomes a pipe table, and an empty title adds no title unit |
| A5 | a table without a header row becomes a pipe table headed by its first row |
| A6 | a pre with a code child and a bare pre both become fenced code units |
| A7 | struck-through text is doubled tildes and a task list keeps its checkboxes |
| A8 | inline elements with no markdown form keep only their text |
| A9 | a plain paragraph converts unchanged |
| A16 | is reported with its position and path, its list and the whole-list rule, and returns no units |
| A17 | is reported alongside the leftover text in one report |
| A25 | stays one unit with its code blocks fenced inside, and passes the fence check |
| A26 | stays one unit with the image as markdown inside its item |
| A19 | the author instruction carries every markdown rule of the recipe contract |
| A20 | the revision instruction carries the same rule text as the author instruction |

The A19 and A20 tests no longer expect the split rule. The tests for A10–A15 and A18 are deleted.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/validate

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/validate.md` if present: it is where a project says how its local system is brought up, which surfaces it has and how each one is reached and authenticated. When it is absent, the project's own setup carries that: its `CLAUDE.md`, its README, its compose or task files. Say what you found before touching anything, and ask when neither says how the system runs.

# Validate

Proves a change against the running system, by hand, after the automated tests have passed. The tests prove the units; this proves the assembled thing does what the design said, through the path a real caller takes.

The rows come from mahou:test-design: every row marked `manual` or both, with its expected outcome and its setup. Without a test design, the user names the scenarios, and the skill records them in the same row shape before running any. The skill adds no scenario of its own.

## Inputs to ask for

Before driving anything, decide whether the surface under validation needs authenticated inputs, and ask for everything in one round, in plain prose in the reply and never through a tool:

- **An identity**, when the surface needs one: a user, an account, a token. Name the surface and what the identity must be able to reach.
- **The access state** that gates the flow: a record the identity owns, a role, a feature switch.
- **Domain inputs** the change names. Read the project's docs for the kind of input its domain deals with, then ask for concrete values. The docs shape the question; they do not answer it.

A surface that needs none of these skips the ask. Do not mine the conversation for values the user did not give; the unconditional ask costs less than the recovery.

## The running system

The system is yours to bring up, not the user's. When it is down, say what bringing it up costs and do it following the project's setup once the user confirms. When a credential or a dependency is missing, stop and ask rather than working around it.

Everything runs against the local system only. Never against a production database or a shared environment.

## Mutating data to reach a row

When the existing data does not reach the code path a row exercises, mutate the local data to make it reachable. The discipline:

- **Capture the original value first**, with a read that prints what you are about to overwrite, before any mutating write. The revert depends on it.
- **Pair every mutation with a revert** that restores the captured value verbatim, and run the revert before the run is declared complete.
- Keep the mutation as small as possible: one field on one record.
- Resetting a flow's state between rows follows the same pattern. A flow that only advances one way at the API level may need a direct write to return to an earlier step; capture, mutate, revert.
- Every mutate and revert pair goes at the top of the report, so the user can audit it.

## Running the rows

Load the reference for the surface under validation:

- [references/browser.md](references/browser.md) for a surface a person drives in a browser.
- [references/http.md](references/http.md) for an API driven with `curl`.

When a change touches both, load both and run each row against its surface. Follow each row's setup, perform its steps, observe, and record PASS or FAIL with the evidence the reference names. Every row runs, in id order; a failing row is recorded and the run continues.

**Fix nothing during validation.** A failure comes back to the user as a decision, with its evidence. When a failure blocks later rows, say which rows it blocks and ask before skipping them.

## The report

Validation produces a report artifact on disk and a summary in the reply that points at it. The artifact is not optional.

One HTML file per run, in the change's scratch folder at `reports/<surface>/index.html`, per the convention in mahou:basics, with every asset in the same folder referenced by relative path. Self-contained, no external resources. Build it as the rows run, not at the end, so a run that stops half way still leaves what it saw.

In order:

1. **Header**: the change, the branches and commits under validation, how the system was brought up, the identities and inputs used.
2. **Setup and mutations**: every configuration change made for the run and the mutate and revert pair of every record touched, with before and after values.
3. **One section per row**, in the order they ran: the setup the row needed, the steps performed, what was observed, PASS or FAIL, and the evidence in the shape the surface's reference gives.
4. **Summary table**: every row with its result, and the rows that could not be run with the reason.

The reply loads mahou:report and gives: the artifact path, which surfaces were exercised, the rows that passed, every failure stated as a failure with where its evidence sits, and every row not run with why.

## Boundaries

- Do not hand-roll a way to start the system when the project has one; follow its setup.
- Drive an API through the path real callers take. When the project routes traffic through a gateway or a proxy, go through it; hitting a service directly hides routing, auth and middleware bugs.
- Do not invent browser-driving strategies; the browser reference defers to the `agent-browser` CLI's own skill content.
- Do not treat green tests as validation. Both are required, in that order.

--- 0 [paragraph]
# Review Before the Concrete Sets
--- 1 [paragraph]
Why the best review comments arrive before the pull request does, and what that costs a team willing to pay for it.
--- 2 [paragraph]
Every engineering org eventually writes a document called something like _Code Review Guidelines_, and every one of those documents describes review as a gate: a place where bad code is _caught_. That word choice is the whole problem. A gate is something you built once and now stand at, checking papers. It does not participate in the trip; it only decides whether the trip continues. Treat review as a gate for long enough and you get exactly what gates produce — long queues, resentment on both sides of the checkpoint, and a growing incentive to route around it.
--- 3 [paragraph]
## The gatekeeping myth
--- 4 [paragraph]
The myth is comfortable because it assigns roles cleanly. There is an author, who writes; there is a reviewer, who judges; and there is a diff, which is either acceptable or is not. Everyone knows where they stand. The trouble is that the diff already encodes a hundred decisions the reviewer never got to weigh in on — which abstraction to introduce, which invariant to trust, which corner to cut under deadline pressure — and by the time it reaches review, unwinding any one of those decisions costs an afternoon instead of a sentence. The gate does not fix the road; it just measures how far off it the car already is.
--- 5 [paragraph]
None of this is an argument against reviewing diffs. It is an argument against believing that a diff is where the decisive conversation happens. If your best reviewers only ever speak up at that stage, you are hearing their opinions **after** the point where those opinions were cheapest to act on. The good ones know this, which is why they leave comments that read less like verdicts and more like _questions you wish someone had asked **before** the branch existed_.
--- 6 [paragraph]
> A review comment that starts with "why" is doing design work. A review comment that starts with "please" is doing enforcement. Teams that only get the second kind have already lost the first.
--- 7 [paragraph]
That distinction is not cosmetic. It is the difference between a reviewer who is still curious about the problem and one who has already decided the diff is the problem. Once a reviewer commits to the second stance, the exchange stops being a design conversation and turns into a negotiation over how much of the original approach survives — and negotiations, unlike conversations, have losers.
--- 8 [paragraph]
### 1\. Grug brain considered
--- 9 [paragraph]
The [grug brain developer](https://grugbrain.dev) has a simpler theory of review, which is that complexity is the actual enemy and review is just the last checkpoint where a second brain gets to notice it. Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes.
--- 10 [paragraph]
This is not an indictment of any particular reviewer — it is a structural observation about when feedback is cheap and when it is expensive. A comment on a design doc costs a paragraph. The same comment, made three weeks later against a finished diff, costs a rewrite, a re-review, and usually a little bit of the author's goodwill toward the whole practice of code ~~rejection~~ review. Teams that move design conversations earlier are not being process-obsessed; they are just refusing to pay expensive prices for cheap information.
--- 11 [paragraph]
> Consider two teams shipping the same feature. The first team writes the interface on a whiteboard, argues about it for twenty minutes, and only then starts typing. The second team starts typing immediately and argues about the interface three days later, in a pull request, across nine review rounds.
> 
> Both teams end up with roughly the same interface. Only one of them enjoyed getting there.
> 
> > And only one of them will want to do it again next sprint.
--- 12 [paragraph]
The nested point matters more than it looks: the cost of a review culture is not paid in code quality, which tends to converge either way. It is paid in whether people volunteer to go through the process a second time.
--- 13 [paragraph]
> Weeks of coding can save you hours of planning.
--- 14 [paragraph]
A review comment that arrives before the branch exists is worth ten that arrive after.
--- 15 [paragraph]
One engineering manager put it this way during a retro: the pull request is where you find out whether the design conversation happened, not where you have it. If review keeps surfacing structural objections, that is not evidence the reviewers are thorough. It is evidence the design conversation moved to the wrong meeting.
--- 16 [paragraph]
**A short digression on tools**
--- 17 [paragraph]
None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches `unused-import` and a type checker catches a mismatched `Optional[str]`, but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."  
That gap is exactly where a design conversation earns its keep, so treat it as a distinct activity rather than a slower version of linting.
--- 18 [paragraph]
People occasionally write the literal string `<software>` in a design doc as a placeholder for whichever service is under discussion, and reviewers reading it later sometimes assume it is a real tag that got mangled by a broken template. It is not; it is a deliberate stand-in, same as writing `3 < 4 and 5 > 2` to illustrate that a comparison operator survived a lossy copy-paste. Neither example is a rendering bug. Both are exactly what the author typed.
--- 19 [paragraph]
#### Lists, structure, and the shape of an explanation
--- 20 [paragraph]
A design conversation eventually needs to produce something the team can point at, and lists are the cheapest way to do that. Here is a plain enumeration of what changes when review moves earlier:
--- 21 [paragraph]
-   Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
-   Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.
-   Authors stop treating reviewers as opponents, because the reviewer was part of the plan, not just its judge.
--- 22 [paragraph]
Compare that with the ordered sequence a team actually follows when adopting the practice:
--- 23 [paragraph]
1.  Write the interface, not the implementation, and share it before any code exists.
2.  Get one reviewer to argue with the interface, not the prose describing it.
3.  Only then let someone start typing the implementation.
--- 24 [paragraph]
Teams that already had four steps before this one keep their own numbering, which is why some retros number their action items starting mid-sequence:
--- 25 [paragraph]
5.  Add the interface decision to the team's running design log.
6.  Revisit it once, after the first real usage, not before.
--- 26 [paragraph]
The nesting gets more elaborate once a team tries to capture both the review checklist and the exceptions to it:
--- 27 [paragraph]
-   Mechanical checks
    1.  Formatting and linting
        -   Auto-fixed on save
        -   Blocking only if auto-fix fails
    2.  Type checking
        -   Blocking in CI
        -   Never waived, even for a hotfix
-   Judgment checks
    1.  Does the interface match the design doc
    2.  Does the change need a design doc it does not have
        -   If yes, review pauses and a doc gets written first
--- 28 [paragraph]
Some list items need more than a sentence, and forcing them into one loses the point:
--- 29 [paragraph]
-   Reviewers who ask for a design doc after the fact are not being obstructive. They are recovering, late, the conversation that should have happened before the branch existed.
    
    The cost of that recovery is real, but it is still cheaper than merging a structural mistake and discovering it during an incident review instead.
    
-   Sometimes the right response to a large diff is not a list of comments but a short script that reproduces the reviewer's concern directly:
    
    ```python
    def has_blocking_comment(review):
        return any(c.severity == "block" for c in review.comments)
    ```
    
    Attaching a failing example is worth more than describing one, because the author can run it immediately.
--- 30 [paragraph]
Some checklists arrive already fragmented, pasted out of a chat thread by whoever was taking notes, and the fragments only make sense read together:
--- 31 [paragraph]
-   a linter that
-   catches syntax
-   but never catches intent
--- 32 [paragraph]
Other lists are the opposite: each item is a small essay on its own, and splitting them further would only lose the argument each one is making.
--- 33 [paragraph]
1.  A design conversation held before code exists changes the cost curve of every disagreement that follows, because an interface is cheap to redraw and a merged abstraction is not; teams that skip this step are not saving time, they are borrowing it at a rate set by however long the abstraction survives in production.
2.  A review culture that only ever produces blocking comments teaches authors to under-scope their pull requests defensively, splitting one coherent change into five defensible ones purely to reduce the surface area any single reviewer can object to, which is a rational response to an irrational incentive.
3.  A team that writes its design decisions down, even briefly, stops re-litigating them every time a new engineer encounters the same tradeoff, because the record answers the question before it gets asked out loud a second time.
--- 34 [paragraph]
Some teams track the vocabulary of review itself as a small glossary:
--- 35 [paragraph]
And some teams track the same rollout as a literal checklist:
--- 36 [paragraph]
-   [x]  Design doc reviewed by at least one other engineer
-   [x]  Interface frozen before implementation started
-   [ ]  Retro scheduled for one sprint after ship
--- 37 [paragraph]
Occasionally the same list shows up copy-pasted from a slide deck, bullet characters and all:
--- 38 [paragraph]
• Move the argument earlier
--- 39 [paragraph]
• Keep the diff boring
--- 40 [paragraph]
• Save the interesting conversation for the doc, not the patch
--- 41 [paragraph]
##### A note on tables
--- 42 [paragraph]
Numbers make the earlier point harder to wave away. One team's review metrics, before and after moving the design conversation earlier:
--- 43 [paragraph]
| Review type | Median time to merge | Defects escaping to production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gate-style (review after code) | 4.2 days | 11 per quarter |
| Design-first (review before code) | 1.6 days | 4 per quarter |
--- 44 [paragraph]
A second table, borrowed from an internal wiki page, never got a header row added — its first row of plain cells has been doing that job for two years:
--- 45 [paragraph]
| Tool | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linter | Fast, deterministic | Blind to intent |
| Type checker | Catches shape mismatches | Blind to whether the shape should exist |
--- 46 [paragraph]
A third table carries its own formatting, because the practices it compares deserve more than plain text:
--- 47 [paragraph]
| Practice | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Design doc first** | Write the interface before the implementation; see the [RFC tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_Comments) this borrows from. |
| _Pairing on the interface_ | Two engineers argue about the shape of a function before either writes its body. |
--- 48 [paragraph]
###### Media and diagrams
--- 49 [paragraph]
A rough sketch of where the conversation moves, compared to where the code review sits:
--- 50 [image] src=https://picsum.photos/seed/review-timeline/800/500 alt='Timeline showing design conversation happening before code, and review shrinking to a final check'
Timeline showing design conversation happening before code, and review shrinking to a final check
--- 51 [image] src=https://picsum.photos/seed/lazyloaded-diagram/800/500 alt='Diagram of a pull request shrinking over successive quarters'
Diagram of a pull request shrinking over successive quarters
--- 52 [paragraph]
A minimal inline diagram of the same idea, built as a small vector drawing rather than a photo:
--- 53 [image] src= alt='Boxes labeled Design, Code, Review connected left to right by arrows'
Boxes labeled Design, Code, Review connected left to right by arrows
--- 54 [paragraph]
Below is the same three-stage pipeline, this time rendered as a syntax-highlighted listing built entirely out of `span` elements rather than a `pre` block, the way some static-site generators produce "copyable" code snippets:
--- 55 [code]
```
def review_stage(diff):
    if diff.has_design_doc:
        return "fast"
    return "slow"
```
--- 56 [paragraph]
And here is a bare terminal transcript, with no code fence at all, exactly as it was pasted from a shell:
--- 57 [code]
```
$ git log --oneline -3
a1b2c3d review: shrink diff after design doc alignment
9f8e7d6 design: freeze queue interface before implementation
1234567 chore: add design-doc template
```
--- 58 [paragraph]
❦
--- 59 [paragraph]
There is a version of this essay that fits in one paragraph, and it is worth writing down for anyone who stopped reading before now. A reviewer's comment is worth roughly 1/2n of its original value after n days of code already written on top of the decision it is objecting to. That is not a precise claim — nobody has actually measured the decay constant — but the shape of the curve matches what every engineer who has requested a late rewrite already knows by feel.
--- 60 [paragraph]
The same relationship, written out as a standalone formula rather than folded into a sentence:
--- 61 [paragraph]
value(comment) = value_0 * 2^{-days_since_decision}
--- 62 [paragraph]
> **If you want the one-sentence version**
> 
> Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.
--- 63 [paragraph]
None of this means review disappears. It means the pull request inherits a smaller job: confirm that the implementation matches the interface everyone already agreed on, catch the mechanical issues a machine would have caught anyway, and leave a paper trail. That is a much less romantic job than "gatekeeper of quality," but it is one a team can actually sustain, sprint after sprint, without anyone quietly starting to dread the review queue.

The second team starts typing immediately and argues about the interface three days later, in a pull request, across nine review rounds.
> 
> Both teams end up with roughly the same interface. Only one of them enjoyed getting there.
> 
> > And only one of them will want to do it again next sprint.
--- 12 [paragraph]
The nested point matters more than it looks: the cost of a review culture is not paid in code quality, which tends to converge either way. It is paid in whether people volunteer to go through the process a second time.
--- 13 [paragraph]
> Weeks of coding can save you hours of planning.
--- 14 [paragraph]
A review comment that arrives before the branch exists is worth ten that arrive after.
--- 15 [paragraph]
One engineering manager put it this way during a retro: the pull request is where you find out whether the design conversation happened, not where you have it. If review keeps surfacing structural objections, that is not evidence the reviewers are thorough. It is evidence the design conversation moved to the wrong meeting.
--- 16 [paragraph]
**A short digression on tools**
--- 17 [paragraph]
None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches `unused-import` and a type checker catches a mismatched `Optional[str]`, but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."  
That gap is exactly where a design conversation earns its keep, so treat it as a distinct activity rather than a slower version of linting.
--- 18 [paragraph]
People occasionally write the literal string `<software>` in a design doc as a placeholder for whichever service is under discussion, and reviewers reading it later sometimes assume it is a real tag that got mangled by a broken template. It is not; it is a deliberate stand-in, same as writing `3 < 4 and 5 > 2` to illustrate that a comparison operator survived a lossy copy-paste. Neither example is a rendering bug. Both are exactly what the author typed.
--- 19 [paragraph]
#### Lists, structure, and the shape of an explanation
--- 20 [paragraph]
A design conversation eventually needs to produce something the team can point at, and lists are the cheapest way to do that. Here is a plain enumeration of what changes when review moves earlier:
--- 21 [paragraph]
-   Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
-   Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.
-   Authors stop treating reviewers as opponents, because the reviewer was part of the plan, not just its judge.
--- 22 [paragraph]
Compare that with the ordered sequence a team actually follows when adopting the practice:
--- 23 [paragraph]
1.  Write the interface, not the implementation, and share it before any code exists.
2.  Get one reviewer to argue with the interface, not the prose describing it.
3.  Only then let someone start typing the implementation.
--- 24 [paragraph]
Teams that already had four steps before this one keep their own numbering, which is why some retros number their action items starting mid-sequence:
--- 25 [paragraph]
5.  Add the interface decision to the team's running design log.
6.  Revisit it once, after the first real usage, not before.
--- 26 [paragraph]
The nesting gets more elaborate once a team tries to capture both the review checklist and the exceptions to it:
--- 27 [paragraph]
-   Mechanical checks
    1.  Formatting and linting
        -   Auto-fixed on save
        -   Blocking only if auto-fix fails
    2.  Type checking
        -   Blocking in CI
        -   Never waived, even for a hotfix
-   Judgment checks
    1.  Does the interface match the design doc
    2.  Does the change need a design doc it does not have
        -   If yes, review pauses and a doc gets written first
--- 28 [paragraph]
Some list items need more than a sentence, and forcing them into one loses the point:
--- 29 [paragraph]
-   Reviewers who ask for a design doc after the fact are not being obstructive. They are recovering, late, the conversation that should have happened before the branch existed.
    
    The cost of that recovery is real, but it is still cheaper than merging a structural mistake and discovering it during an incident review instead.
    
-   Sometimes the right response to a large diff is not a list of comments but a short script that reproduces the reviewer's concern directly:
    
    ```python
    def has_blocking_comment(review):
        return any(c.severity == "block" for c in review.comments)
    ```
    
    Attaching a failing example is worth more than describing one, because the author can run it immediately.
--- 30 [paragraph]
Some checklists arrive already fragmented, pasted out of a chat thread by whoever was taking notes, and the fragments only make sense read together:
--- 31 [paragraph]
-   a linter that
-   catches syntax
-   but never catches intent
--- 32 [paragraph]
Other lists are the opposite: each item is a small essay on its own, and splitting them further would only lose the argument each one is making.
--- 33 [paragraph]
1.  A design conversation held before code exists changes the cost curve of every disagreement that follows, because an interface is cheap to redraw and a merged abstraction is not; teams that skip this step are not saving time, they are borrowing it at a rate set by however long the abstraction survives in production.
2.  A review culture that only ever produces blocking comments teaches authors to under-scope their pull requests defensively, splitting one coherent change into five defensible ones purely to reduce the surface area any single reviewer can object to, which is a rational response to an irrational incentive.
3.  A team that writes its design decisions down, even briefly, stops re-litigating them every time a new engineer encounters the same tradeoff, because the record answers the question before it gets asked out loud a second time.
--- 34 [paragraph]
Some teams track the vocabulary of review itself as a small glossary:
--- 35 [paragraph]
And some teams track the same rollout as a literal checklist:
--- 36 [paragraph]
-   [x]  Design doc reviewed by at least one other engineer
-   [x]  Interface frozen before implementation started
-   [ ]  Retro scheduled for one sprint after ship
--- 37 [paragraph]
Occasionally the same list shows up copy-pasted from a slide deck, bullet characters and all:
--- 38 [paragraph]
• Move the argument earlier
--- 39 [paragraph]
• Keep the diff boring
--- 40 [paragraph]
• Save the interesting conversation for the doc, not the patch
--- 41 [paragraph]
##### A note on tables
--- 42 [paragraph]
Numbers make the earlier point harder to wave away. One team's review metrics, before and after moving the design conversation earlier:
--- 43 [paragraph]
| Review type | Median time to merge | Defects escaping to production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gate-style (review after code) | 4.2 days | 11 per quarter |
| Design-first (review before code) | 1.6 days | 4 per quarter |
--- 44 [paragraph]
A second table, borrowed from an internal wiki page, never got a header row added — its first row of plain cells has been doing that job for two years:
--- 45 [paragraph]
| Tool | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linter | Fast, deterministic | Blind to intent |
| Type checker | Catches shape mismatches | Blind to whether the shape should exist |
--- 46 [paragraph]
A third table carries its own formatting, because the practices it compares deserve more than plain text:
--- 47 [paragraph]
| Practice | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Design doc first** | Write the interface before the implementation; see the [RFC tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_Comments) this borrows from. |
| _Pairing on the interface_ | Two engineers argue about the shape of a function before either writes its body. |
--- 48 [paragraph]
###### Media and diagrams
--- 49 [paragraph]
A rough sketch of where the conversation moves, compared to where the code review sits:
--- 50 [image] src=https://picsum.photos/seed/review-timeline/800/500 alt='Timeline showing design conversation happening before code, and review shrinking to a final check'

--- 51 [image] src=https://picsum.photos/seed/lazyloaded-diagram/800/500 alt='Diagram of a pull request shrinking over successive quarters'

A minimal inline diagram of the same idea, built as a small vector drawing rather than a photo:
--- 53 [image] src= alt='Boxes labeled Design, Code, Review connected left to right by arrows'
Boxes labeled Design, Code, Review connected left to right by arrows
--- 54 [paragraph]
Below is the same three-stage pipeline, this time rendered as a syntax-highlighted listing built entirely out of `span` elements rather than a `pre` block, the way some static-site generators produce "copyable" code snippets:
--- 55 [code]
```
def review_stage(diff):
    if diff.has_design_doc:
        return "fast"
    return "slow"
```
--- 56 [paragraph]
And here is a bare terminal transcript, with no code fence at all, exactly as it was pasted from a shell:
--- 57 [code]
```
$ git log --oneline -3

9f8e7d6 design: freeze queue interface before implementation
1234567 chore: add design-doc template
```
--- 58 [paragraph]
❦
--- 59 [paragraph]
There is a version of this essay that fits in one paragraph, and it is worth writing down for anyone who stopped reading before now. A reviewer's comment is worth roughly 1/2n of its original value after n days of code already written on top of the decision it is objecting to. That is not a precise claim — nobody has actually measured the decay constant — but the shape of the curve matches what every engineer who has requested a late rewrite already knows by feel.
--- 60 [paragraph]
The same relationship, written out as a standalone formula rather than folded into a sentence:
--- 61 [paragraph]
value(comment) = value_0 * 2^{-days_since_decision}
--- 62 [paragraph]
> **If you want the one-sentence version**
> 
> Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.
--- 63 [paragraph]
None of this means review disappears. It means the pull request inherits a smaller job: confirm that the implementation matches the interface everyone already agreed on, catch the mechanical issues a machine would have caught anyway, and leave a paper trail. That is a much less romantic job than "gatekeeper of quality," but it is one a team can actually sustain, sprint after sprint, without anyone quietly starting to dread the review queue.

content.text:
A16 passes and A25 fails on one construct: inline formulas. Evidence report: `.scratch/markdown-and-lists/reports/validate-pipeline/index.html`, with the requests, responses and workflow step outputs beside it. I ran both rows against the local pipeline only (`pnpm dev`, `POST /jobs` and `GET /jobs/`). That was two jobs with real AI Gateway calls, no production data touched, and the dev server is stopped. | Row | Result | Evidence | |---|---|---| | A16 | PASS | `a16-workflow-instance.json`, `a16-result.json`, `a16-settled-recipe.js` | | A25 | FAIL | `a25-result.json`, `a25-recipe.js`, per-construct table in `index.html` | **A16.** The stored per-`
  • ` recipe failed validation with four orphaned-`
  • ` report lines, one per list item. - Each line names the unit by position and path, the `
      ` it belongs to, and the whole-list rule. - The revision agent settled on its first attempt. The new recipe declares `ul` as a unit and no longer iterates over the `
    • ` elements. - The job completed with 5 units: `# ` first, then the list as one unit with `-` markers. **A25.** The author agent settled on its first attempt and the job completed with 64 units. These came out as expected: - `# <title>` first, and the source `<h1>` is not repeated. - Headings `##` to `######`, with the heading self-link dropped. - Quotes carry `>`, including a nested quote, and the attribution is left out. - `start="5"` is kept. - All three tables are pipe tables, including the one with no header row. - `~~rejection~~`, and the task list keeps `[x]` / `[ ]`. - The list holding a Python code block is one unit with the fence inside it. - No unit is a lone `<li>`. - The `<dl>`, the footnote markers and the footnote list are left out. - The block formula is its alttext with no `$`. The row fails on this: - **Inline formulas came out wrong.** `<math alttext="1/2^n">` inside a `<p>` reached the unit as `1/2n`, its MathML text, instead of `1/2^n`, its alttext. The authored recipe swaps only `<math>` elements that are direct children of the container, so inline ones go through `toMarkdown` untouched. The contract says a formula is its alttext, but the author agent applied that only to block formulas. And one construct could not be checked: - **A list holding an image did not appear.** No `<li>` in the synthetic article contains an image. A26's automated test is the only evidence for it. The recipe the agent wrote emits the `<svg>` as an image unit with an empty `src` and its `aria-label` as alt. That is the recipe's own choice; no runtime code treats `<svg>` specially.
